analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal compensation fund for firefighters sickened by PFAS "forever chemicals," paid for by a 10% tax on PFAS product sales and PFAS lawsuit settlements.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to House committees in March 2024, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Firefighters are exposed to PFAS ("forever chemicals") in their protective gear and firefighting foam, and studies have linked that exposure to several cancers. This bill would have set up a no-fault federal program paying firefighters or their families $250,000 for PFAS-linked cancer and $50,000 for other PFAS-linked conditions, scaled up for years of service. The money would come from a new trust fund filled by a 10% excise tax on PFAS products sold by manufacturers and a 10% tax on PFAS lawsuit settlement payments. The bill was referred to three House committees, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Firefighters (career, military, and volunteer) with at least two years of service who suffer PFAS-linked cancers or other conditions, and their surviving families, who could receive a set federal payment without having to sue a chemical company or prove which manufacturer's product made them sick. The payouts would be funded by PFAS manufacturers and companies paying PFAS lawsuit settlements.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a no-fault compensation program that automatically presumes a firefighter's PFAS-related illness was caused by exposure on the job, so claimants do not have to prove who made the chemicals or who was negligent.
Sets a base award of $250,000 for cancer and $50,000 for other PFAS-related conditions, multiplied up to 4x for long-serving firefighters, with appeals allowed in federal court.
Caps attorneys' fees and shields compensation from the deceased firefighter's creditors.

analysis.who_pays: PFAS manufacturers, importers, and sellers, who would pay a 10% excise tax on PFAS product sales, plus parties paying PFAS lawsuit settlements, who would pay a 10% litigation excise tax. Some of the product tax could be passed on in prices.

drawbacks.text: The program pays out only from the PFAS Trust Fund, which depends on the new 10% excise taxes and annual appropriations; if funding is insufficient, payments would be prorated (reduced) until money becomes available.
The no-fault rule presumes any listed PFAS-related condition was caused by firefighting exposure, which speeds claims for sick firefighters but sidesteps individual causation questions.
A 10% tax on PFAS product sales and on PFAS litigation settlements would raise costs for manufacturers and for parties settling PFAS lawsuits, some of which could be passed along.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On the merits, the bill offered a real benefit — no-fault compensation for firefighters whose cancer likely came from job exposures — funded by the industries that sold PFAS products and face PFAS lawsuits. Drawbacks: the trust fund could be insufficient, forcing prorated payments; a 10% tax on PFAS products would raise costs for manufacturers, and some of that cost could be passed on to buyers of everyday PFAS-containing products; and the 10% tax on litigation settlement proceeds effectively skimmed money owed to injured parties. It never advanced far enough for Congress to weigh these trade-offs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced and a subcommittee the next day, but none of them acted on it, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Darren Soto introduced the Firefighter PFAS Injury Compensation Act of 2024 on March 21, 2024.
It was referred to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Budget Committees, then to a Health subcommittee on March 22, 2024.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded; the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers and large PFAS litigation defendants — they avoided a 10% tax on their products and settlements and kept facing individual lawsuits rather than a federal compensation fund.

for.name: Rep. Darren Soto
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 21, 2024; it was referred to three committees and never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: With zero cosponsors and no committee action, no votes were ever recorded, so the partisan shape of support is unknown.

industries.industry: PFAS manufacturers and companies that make or sell PFAS-containing products
industries.note: The bill would impose a 10% excise tax on every PFAS product sold, including firefighting gear, to fund compensation for sick firefighters [S2].

industries.industry: PFAS litigation defendants (chemical companies and other large settlement payers)
industries.note: The bill would take a 10% cut of PFAS lawsuit settlements and awards to fund the trust fund, adding to the industry's growing legal liabilities [S2].
Gear containing PFAS would face the same 10% sales tax, raising costs for fire departments, while firefighters themselves would be the program's beneficiaries [S2].
